paragraphs: This paper improves how Dempster–Shafer evidence theory models uncertain information. The authors identify two problems in existing approaches: they can overlook prior information already present in the data, and imbalanced data can cause important information to receive too little attention. Their proposed learning strategy adjusts how evidence contributes to the model as learning proceeds.

The framework combines two mechanisms. Nonuniform splitting dynamically changes the weights assigned to subsets of data, while a diffusion factor helps incorporate prior information. Together, these components aim to handle uncertainty and conflicting evidence more flexibly. A mapping into a Hilbert space provides a second way to reduce conflict when different pieces of information are combined.

Experiments across multiple tasks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, including better classification and low-light image enhancement. The contribution connects uncertainty modeling with practical prediction and image processing: changing how evidence is weighted and reconciled can improve the resulting outputs. The reported benefits apply to the evaluated tasks, where the combined strategy performed better than the compared alternatives.
neurips-2025-a-dynamic-learning-strategy.tldr: A dynamic evidence-learning strategy uses adaptive weighting and Hilbert space mapping to improve uncertainty handling, classification, and low-light image enhancement.

paragraphs: This paper benchmarks whether large language models can improve recommendations compared with conventional recommendation systems. It examines two tasks: predicting whether someone will click an item and recommending items from a sequence of previous interactions. The evaluation also varies how items are represented, including unique identifiers, text, semantic embeddings, and semantic identifiers.

The experiments cover up to 17 large models and five datasets spanning fashion, news, video, books, and music. This design makes the comparison broader than a single application or a single way of presenting items. It examines recommendation quality across both the information given to a model and the type of prediction the model must produce.

The authors report improvements of up to 5% in AUC for click prediction and up to 170% in NDCG@10 for sequential recommendation. These are the largest reported gains, rather than improvements guaranteed across settings. They come with substantially slower inference, which the authors judge impractical for real-time recommendation. The central finding is therefore a quality–efficiency tradeoff: stronger recommendations in the evaluation require much more costly prediction.
neurips-2025-can-llms-outshine-conventio.tldr: LLM recommenders achieve substantial quality gains in the benchmark, but their slow inference makes the evaluated approach impractical for real-time recommendations.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series contain several channels of measurements evolving together. This paper asks how information in individual channels affects a trained model's performance. It builds on influence functions, which estimate the consequences of changing training data without repeatedly carrying out expensive retraining. The authors argue that this channel-level perspective has received too little attention.

Their method, Channel-wise Influence, or ChInf, estimates influence separately for different channels. This makes it possible to investigate counterfactual questions about how changing channel information would affect the model. The authors also incorporate ChInf into two algorithms for established time-series tasks, connecting the interpretability method to concrete improvements in analysis.

Experiments evaluate anomaly detection and data pruning, where the aim is respectively to find unusual behavior and select training data. The ChInf-based methods rank first among the compared methods, while earlier influence functions perform poorly on these tasks. These findings support the value of accounting explicitly for channel information in the evaluated settings, rather than assuming existing influence estimates transfer effectively to multivariate time series.
neurips-2025-channel-matters-estimating-.tldr: ChInf estimates how individual time-series channels influence models and improves anomaly detection and data pruning in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasts need uncertainty estimates that remain useful when the process being observed changes. A change point is a sudden shift in that underlying process. The paper addresses a weakness of existing conformal prediction methods: their difficulty handling these shifts, even though conformal prediction is otherwise a general and efficient approach to uncertainty quantification.

The proposed CPTC algorithm combines a model that predicts the underlying state with online conformal prediction. The state prediction component accounts for which conditions the series is operating under, while the online component models uncertainty as observations arrive. This combination targets non-stationary series, whose behavior changes over time, rather than treating past observations as coming from one unchanged process.

The authors prove validity and improved adaptivity under assumptions described as minimal. They also evaluate CPTC on six synthetic and real-world datasets, reporting better validity and adaptivity than state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution concerns both dependable uncertainty estimates and their ability to respond to changing conditions, with theoretical analysis and experiments supporting the proposed combination.
neurips-2025-conformal-prediction-for-ti.tldr: CPTC combines state prediction with online conformal prediction to improve uncertainty validity and adaptation in time series with sudden changes.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models generate sequences by repeatedly removing categorical noise. This paper uses that iterative generation process to enforce requirements on the sequence as a whole. Such requirements can include logical rules, safety conditions, or desired properties. The aim is to make those requirements part of generation itself, reducing reliance on filtering completed outputs or retraining a model.

The proposed method, Constrained Discrete Diffusion, integrates differentiable constraint optimization into diffusion sampling. Constraints therefore guide the evolving sequence while it is being produced. The method is training-free, so its control mechanism operates during sampling. This is particularly relevant when an output must satisfy explicit requirements while still remaining useful as a generated text or molecule.

Experiments cover toxicity-controlled text, molecules with specified properties, and text completion subject to instructions. Across the evaluated tasks, the authors report zero constraint violations while preserving fluency, novelty, and coherence, and outperforming compared autoregressive and discrete diffusion approaches. Zero violations is the reported experimental outcome; the finding demonstrates strong constraint adherence in those evaluations alongside retained generation quality.
neurips-2025-constrained-discrete-diffus.tldr: CDD embeds constraint optimization into discrete diffusion sampling and reports zero violations across evaluated text and molecule generation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops reinforcement learning for control problems in which states and actions evolve continuously under stochastic differential equations. Most reinforcement learning methods instead use discrete time steps. The central challenge here is retaining a Q-function's ability to evaluate actions while formulating the learning problem directly in continuous time.

The authors characterize continuous-time Q-functions through a martingale condition and use dynamic programming to connect a diffusion policy's score with the action gradient of a learned Q-function. That gradient describes how the Q-function changes as the action changes. The connection motivates Continuous Q-Score Matching, an algorithm that improves the policy through score matching while retaining action evaluation without relying on time discretization.

The paper also derives closed-form solutions for linear-quadratic control problems within its framework. Numerical experiments in simulated environments demonstrate the method's effectiveness and compare it with popular baselines. The contribution combines a continuous-time account of action value with a practical policy improvement method, supported by analytical results for a specific control class and empirical results in simulation.
neurips-2025-continuous-q-score-matching.tldr: CQSM links continuous-time Q-functions to diffusion policy scores, enabling policy improvement while preserving action evaluation without time discretization.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings used to solve partial differential equations, but acquiring high-quality training data can be expensive and constrained by resolution. DeltaPhi addresses this shortage by changing the learning target. Rather than learning only a direct mapping from an input state to its output, the framework learns differences between similar physical states.

The approach exploits stability in physical systems: nearby initial states lead to nearby evolution trajectories. Learning these residual differences provides implicit data augmentation, extracting training value from relationships among states. This stability property is central to the motivation for the reformulation. DeltaPhi is also architecture-agnostic, allowing it to enhance existing neural operators without requiring one particular network design.

Experiments report consistent, significant improvements across diverse physical systems, regular and irregular domains, multiple neural architectures, different training-data quantities, and changes in resolution. These results support residual learning as a broadly useful enhancement in the evaluated data-limited settings. The main idea is to make better use of scarce physical examples by learning how related states differ as they evolve.
neurips-2025-deltaphi-physical-states-re.tldr: DeltaPhi improves neural operators with limited training data by learning differences between similar physical states and exploiting stable evolution.

paragraphs: This paper studies how useful information develops during a large reasoning model's generated reasoning. The authors track mutual information between intermediate representations and the correct answer. This quantity captures how much information those representations contain about the answer. They observe sudden increases at particular generation steps, suggesting that information gain is unevenly distributed across the reasoning sequence.

The authors theoretically analyze these peaks and show a relationship in which increasing mutual information decreases prediction error probability. Empirically, the peaks often align with words marking reflection or transition, such as “Hmm,” “Wait,” and “Therefore.” They call these thinking tokens and demonstrate that these tokens are crucial to reasoning performance in their analyses, while other tokens have minimal effects.

Building on these observations, the paper introduces two methods that use thinking tokens to improve reasoning performance. The findings connect changes inside the model with recognizable transitions in its generated reasoning. They also motivate a targeted route to improvement: exploiting particular moments associated with increased answer information, instead of treating every part of a reasoning sequence as equally consequential.
neurips-2025-demystifying-reasoning-dyna.tldr: The paper links sudden increases in answer-related information to thinking tokens and uses those tokens in two methods that improve reasoning.

paragraphs: The Distance-informed Neural Process aims to make predictions with uncertainty estimates that better reflect the available data. Standard Neural Processes often summarize a task through a global latent variable. The authors identify two weaknesses in that approach: difficulty calibrating uncertainty and insufficient modeling of local relationships between inputs.

DNP retains a global variable for variation across tasks and adds a local variable that captures input similarity. It uses bi-Lipschitz regularization to bound how much relationships between inputs can be distorted in the learned representation. This encourages relative distances to remain meaningful, allowing the local component to use proximity information alongside the broader task-level description.

The authors report strong predictive performance and improved uncertainty calibration on regression and classification tasks. They also find that the approach more effectively distinguishes data within the training distribution from data outside it. The contribution is a way to combine global context with local similarity so that uncertainty reflects both. Preserving useful distance relationships is the mechanism connecting that modeling choice to the reported improvements.
neurips-2025-distance-informed-neural-pr.tldr: DNP combines global and distance-aware local latent variables to improve uncertainty calibration and distinguish familiar from out-of-distribution data.

paragraphs: DrVD-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models ground medical reasoning in images and follow processes resembling clinical reasoning. The motivation is that promising medical-image answers do not by themselves establish that a model understands the visual evidence. A model may instead exploit superficial patterns that produce plausible responses without the intended reasoning.

The benchmark contains 7,789 image–question pairs across 20 task types, 17 diagnostic categories, and five imaging modalities: CT, MRI, ultrasound, radiography, and pathology. Its three modules assess visual evidence comprehension, reasoning trajectories, and report generation. Tasks follow a clinical workflow from recognizing the imaging modality through identifying lesions and making a diagnosis.

The authors evaluate 19 models spanning general-purpose and medical systems, as well as open-source and proprietary offerings. Performance falls sharply as reasoning becomes more complex. Some models show signs of human-like reasoning, but they often still depend on shortcut correlations rather than grounded visual understanding. The benchmark makes this gap visible by examining intermediate evidence and reasoning, providing a structured basis for developing more clinically trustworthy models.
neurips-2025-drvd-bench-do-vision-langua.tldr: DrVD-Bench finds that evaluated vision-language models struggle as clinical reasoning grows more complex and often rely on shortcut correlations.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when feedback consists of preferences between entire trajectories rather than numerical rewards. The agent must choose which pairs of experiences to compare so that the feedback reveals the underlying reward efficiently. The setting covers general Markov decision processes, making informative query selection a central algorithmic problem.

The authors propose a meta-algorithm based on randomized exploration that avoids computational difficulties associated with optimistic approaches. Under mild assumptions about access to a reinforcement learning oracle, they establish guarantees for regret and for the final policy produced. An improved version collects batches of trajectory pairs and uses optimal experimental design to choose informative comparisons, reducing the number of preference queries needed.

Batching also allows several feedback requests to be answered concurrently, a practical advantage when gathering preferences. Empirical evaluation finds the method competitive with reinforcement learning that receives rewards directly, despite using few preference queries. The contribution joins tractable exploration, principled query selection, and theoretical guarantees, showing how an agent can make more effective use of limited comparison feedback.
neurips-2025-efficient-preference-based-.tldr: Randomized exploration and experimental design enable theoretically supported reinforcement learning with a small number of informative trajectory-preference queries.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be expensive to train because their deep stacks process information through many layers. This paper investigates whether all layers continue to need the same treatment throughout training. It connects self-attention with modern Hopfield networks, using the perspective of energy-based memory systems to study how layer behavior evolves.

The authors introduce the Layer Instability Index, a measure derived from the operational softmax mode and its variability. It quantifies each layer's metastability over time. Their analysis finds that some layers repeatedly settle into attractor-like states, suggesting early stabilization and functional specialization. Based on this behavior, an adaptive training framework dynamically freezes or skips layers identified as stable.

Experiments span small, base, and large Vision Transformers across several image-classification datasets, including CUB-200-2011, CIFAR-10/100, Food-101, Stanford Dogs, and Beans. The approach reduces training costs while maintaining or improving accuracy in these evaluations. The findings suggest that observed layer dynamics can guide where training computation is spent, using signs of stabilization to avoid unnecessary work.
neurips-2025-energy-landscape-aware-visi.tldr: An energy-based measure of layer stability guides freezing or skipping in Vision Transformers, reducing training cost while maintaining or improving evaluated accuracy.

paragraphs: Monocular depth estimation predicts scene depth from a single image. Although large models have improved substantially on standard benchmarks, this paper argues that accuracy scores leave an important question unanswered: how reliably do predictions hold up when the scene changes? A model's success on fixed benchmark images provides only a partial assessment of that robustness.

The authors introduce Procedural Depth Evaluation, or PDE, to study this question systematically. It generates three-dimensional scenes procedurally and applies controlled changes to objects, cameras, materials, and lighting. Because the evaluation explicitly varies these aspects of scene content, it can investigate sensitivity to particular kinds of change rather than combining them into one overall accuracy result.

The analysis identifies perturbations that challenge state-of-the-art depth models. The contribution is a benchmark for examining how changes in a constructed scene affect depth prediction, complementing conventional accuracy evaluation. Its controlled setup provides a way to study robustness across different sources of visual variation, with the reported findings intended to guide further depth-estimation research.
neurips-2025-evaluating-robustness-of-mo.tldr: PDE uses procedurally generated scenes to test how monocular depth models respond to controlled object, camera, material, and lighting changes.

paragraphs: GOOD generates examples outside a model's familiar data distribution to help improve out-of-distribution detection. Existing diffusion-based approaches often alter text-conditioning embeddings, which can destabilize meaning and produce too little variety in distribution shifts. GOOD instead guides the diffusion sampling trajectory directly, using an existing classifier trained on in-distribution data.

The method combines guidance at two levels. Image-level guidance uses a log-partition gradient to push generated samples toward low-density regions in pixel space. Feature-level guidance uses nearest-neighbor distances in the classifier's internal representation to encourage samples in sparsely populated feature regions. Together, these signals aim to make generated unfamiliar examples both more diverse and more controllable. An additional detection score adaptively combines image and feature discrepancies.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations support the approach, and training with GOOD-generated samples notably improves out-of-distribution detection in the reported experiments. The training-free description applies to the guided sampling framework; the paper also explicitly studies subsequent detector training with its outputs. Its contribution is a way to use existing classifier information to create useful unfamiliar examples and strengthen detection.
neurips-2025-good-training-free-guided-d.tldr: GOOD guides diffusion with image- and feature-level classifier signals to generate diverse unfamiliar samples that improve out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: LooGLE v2 examines whether large language models can use information spread across long real-world texts. Larger context windows allow models to accept more text, but that capacity does not establish that they can understand dependencies throughout it. The benchmark focuses on practical tasks where answering requires handling such long-range relationships.

The dataset contains automatically collected texts ranging from 16,000 to two million tokens across law, finance, games, and code. A scalable curation pipeline produces 1,934 question-answer instances covering ten domain-specific task types with varied complexity. This design evaluates long-context capability through application-oriented questions, making the connection between input length and useful understanding central to the assessment.

The authors test six locally deployed and four API-based models. Even the strongest reaches an overall score of only 59.2%. They conclude that the evaluated models effectively understand much shorter contexts than their advertised windows suggest. The result highlights a practical gap between accepting lengthy inputs and successfully solving tasks that depend on information across those inputs.
neurips-2025-loogle-v2-are-llms-ready-fo.tldr: LooGLE v2 exposes a gap between large advertised context windows and effective long-dependency reasoning, with the best evaluated model scoring 59.2% overall.

paragraphs: PolyGuard evaluates language-model guardrails using risks grounded in authentic safety guidelines for specific domains. The authors argue that ad hoc risk categories can miss operational requirements and overlook how the same risk has different implications in different settings. Their dataset covers eight safety-critical domains, including finance, law, and code generation.

The benchmark includes statements, questions, instructions, and multi-turn conversations. It also contains benign examples curated through detoxification prompting to challenge excessive refusal, alongside adversarial examples designed to bypass safeguards. These components test both sides of guardrail behavior: recognizing problematic interactions and allowing harmless ones, across multiple formats and domain-specific policy requirements.

Evaluation of 19 guardrail models finds substantial variation across risk categories, indicating uneven domain coverage. The authors also observe that newer models can cover more kinds of risk while losing performance on common categories. Every evaluated model remains vulnerable to optimized adversarial attacks. These findings show why policy-grounded, domain-aware evaluation matters: broader coverage alone does not establish consistent performance or resistance to deliberate attempts to evade a guardrail.
neurips-2025-polyguard-massive-multi-dom.tldr: PolyGuard benchmarks guardrails against domain-specific safety policies and finds uneven risk coverage and adversarial vulnerabilities across all 19 evaluated models.

paragraphs: Global Covariance Pooling uses second-order feature statistics to build representations for visual recognition. This paper identifies a tension between two approaches to computing it. Newton–Schulz-based iSQRT-COV stabilizes early learning but can excessively compress large eigenvalues later. SVD-based approaches preserve that structure better, yet small gaps between eigenvalues can make early training unstable.

Halley-SVD uses a higher-order iterative method to combine smooth gradients with preservation of important spectral structure. Its formulation avoids explicit division by differences between eigenvalues and does not require threshold or polynomial heuristics. The aim is to prevent early gradient explosions while also avoiding the later over-flattening that can stall final accuracy.

Experiments on convolutional networks and transformers show consistent, robust improvements over iSQRT-COV at large model scales and batch sizes. The method achieves higher accuracy without switching algorithms during training or introducing custom truncations. The findings support a single computational approach that handles both stages of the problem: stable optimization early and faithful retention of large-eigenvalue structure later.
neurips-2025-revitalizing-svd-for-global.tldr: Halley-SVD improves covariance pooling by combining stable early gradients with preservation of large eigenvalues later in training.

paragraphs: ShapeEmbed learns numerical descriptions of object contours in two-dimensional images. Its central goal is to describe shape consistently when an object's position, orientation, or size changes. Without that consistency, measurements can reflect how an object appears in an image rather than the geometric features the analysis is intended to capture.

The framework represents a contour as a Euclidean distance matrix and learns a shape descriptor through self-supervision. The descriptor is invariant to translation, scaling, rotation, reflection, and point indexing. Thus, its intended representation remains unchanged under those transformations, including changes in the ordering used to identify contour points. The method addresses limitations of traditional descriptors and improves on existing autoencoder-based approaches.

In shape-classification experiments on natural and biological images, the learned descriptors outperform competing methods. These results support the usefulness of the representation for distinguishing shapes while discounting the specified transformations. The authors see particular potential in biological imaging, where contour information can be valuable. That application is a proposed area of relevance, alongside the reported classification findings on biological images.
neurips-2025-shapeembed-a-self-supervise.tldr: ShapeEmbed learns contour descriptors invariant to several geometric and indexing transformations, improving shape classification on natural and biological images.

paragraphs: SparseDiff predicts complex systems whose spatial patterns evolve over time. The authors argue that conventional latent representations can discard spatial structure, making it difficult to model interactions or recognize new dynamics during long forecasts. Their approach updates the encoding at test time so that the representation can adapt as the system develops.

A codebook-based sparse encoder first converts the continuous spatial domain into a sparse graph. A graph neural ordinary differential equation models the dynamics on this structure and guides a diffusion decoder that reconstructs the system. During autoregressive prediction, adaptive re-encoding changes the graph topology to accommodate emerging spatiotemporal patterns, rather than keeping the initial structure fixed throughout the forecast.

Across evaluations on representative systems, SparseDiff reports an average prediction-error reduction of 49.99% compared with baselines while requiring only 1% of the spatial resolution. These results support the combination of sparse spatial modeling and ongoing adaptation in the tested systems. The central contribution is making the representation itself responsive to long-term evolution, alongside learning how the represented system changes.
neurips-2025-sparse-diffusion-autoencode.tldr: SparseDiff adapts a sparse graph representation during forecasting, reporting 49.99% lower average prediction error while requiring only 1% of spatial resolution.

paragraphs: SpecReason addresses the latency of large reasoning models that generate long chains of thought. Its motivating observation is that an intermediate reasoning step can be useful because of the idea it contributes, even when its exact wording varies. Complex problems often contain simpler steps that may therefore be handled with a cheaper approximation.

The system delegates those intermediate steps to a lightweight model. The more expensive base model assesses the proposed reasoning and can correct it. This division of work exploits flexibility in the meaning of reasoning text while seeking to preserve final-answer accuracy. It complements speculative decoding, which instead requires token-level equivalence at each step.

Across reasoning benchmarks from multiple domains, SpecReason achieves speedups of 1.4–3.0 times over ordinary large reasoning model inference and reported accuracy improvements of 0.4–9.0%. Combining it with speculative decoding reduces latency by an additional 8.8–58.0% compared with speculative decoding alone. The results support using a smaller model for simpler reasoning while reserving expensive computation for assessment and correction.
neurips-2025-specreason-fast-and-accurat.tldr: SpecReason uses a lightweight model for intermediate reasoning and a larger model for checking, achieving 1.4–3.0× speedups with improved benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning builds representations without labeled examples, often by encouraging transformed versions of an input to receive similar representations. This paper focuses on two properties that help those representations remain useful: avoiding dimensional collapse, where features occupy only a small subspace, and distributing representations more uniformly across the space available to them.

T-REGS introduces a regularization framework based on the length of a minimum spanning tree over learned representations. Such a tree connects the represented points with minimal total edge length. Using its length gives the framework a geometric quantity that reflects relationships across the collection of representations, tying the learning objective to how those points occupy their space.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that T-REGS both mitigates dimensional collapse and promotes uniformity on arbitrary compact Riemannian manifolds. Experiments on synthetic data and standard self-supervised learning benchmarks support improvements in representation quality. The contribution is a simple shared mechanism for addressing both geometric properties, with theory extending beyond an exclusively flat representation-space setting.
neurips-2025-t-regs-minimum-spanning-tre.tldr: T-REGS uses minimum-spanning-tree length to mitigate representation collapse and encourage uniformity, with theoretical analysis and experimental support.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which internal neurons contribute to language-model safety behavior. The authors use inference-time activation contrasting to locate candidate safety neurons, then apply dynamic activation patching to test their causal effects. This moves the analysis from observing internal activity to intervening on it and measuring how safety behavior changes.

Across multiple widely used models, the method consistently identifies about 5% of neurons as safety neurons. Patching only their activations restores over 90% of safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without affecting general ability in the reported experiments. The result suggests that targeted activation changes can recover much of the measured safety behavior without broadly changing the model's capabilities.

The authors also find substantial overlap between neurons important for safety and helpfulness, although the two behaviors require different activation patterns. This offers a mechanistic explanation for the alignment tax: safety and helpfulness can place different demands on shared internal components. Finally, the paper demonstrates an application that uses these findings to detect unsafe outputs before generation, connecting the analysis to a safeguarding mechanism.
neurips-2025-towards-understanding-safet.tldr: Activation interventions identify a small set of safety-related neurons and restore over 90% of measured safety performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: ViewPoint generates immersive 360-degree videos using pretrained diffusion models designed for ordinary perspective video. The challenge is a mismatch between panoramic content and the perspective imagery that dominates modern diffusion-model training. Generating a panorama requires coherent spatial relationships across the full view while retaining the local visual detail learned from perspective data.

The framework introduces a panorama representation called the ViewPoint map, designed to combine global spatial continuity with fine-grained detail. A Pano-Perspective attention mechanism lets the model use its pretrained perspective knowledge while capturing spatial correlations within that representation. Together, these components connect an existing video model's learned visual patterns to the requirements of panoramic generation.

Extensive experiments report highly dynamic, spatially consistent panoramic videos and state-of-the-art performance exceeding previous methods. The contribution is a representation and attention design that makes pretrained perspective models useful for panoramic output. The results support the proposed bridge between the two visual formats, with potential relevance to the panoramic video needs of virtual reality, world models, and spatial intelligence.
neurips-2025-viewpoint-panoramic-video-g.tldr: ViewPoint combines a new panorama representation with specialized attention to generate dynamic, spatially consistent 360-degree videos from pretrained perspective models.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether adding vision-and-language training changes a language model's conceptual knowledge. It focuses on taxonomy: how concepts relate through categories and category membership. The authors compare closely matched text-only models and their vision-language counterparts, then test them on text-only questions that require understanding these relationships.

Vision-language models often answer these questions better. To investigate why, the researchers combine targeted behavioral tests with analyses of internal representations. They find no significant difference in the models' taxonomic knowledge itself. Instead, the models differ in how they represent questions containing taxonomically related concepts compared with questions containing concepts without that relationship.

The findings suggest that additional vision-language training improves access to, or use of, existing taxonomic knowledge within this task, without substantially changing the knowledge itself. This distinction matters when interpreting better task scores: improved performance can reflect better deployment of stored knowledge. The observed benefit also appears when the question is entirely linguistic, showing that the effect of multimodal training can carry into a text-only setting.
neurips-2025-vision-and-language-trainin.tldr: Vision-language training often improves taxonomic question answering by helping models use existing knowledge, without substantially changing that knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which training examples help language models reason in mathematics and programming. Its Influence-based Reasoning Attribution method, Infra, uses influence functions to attribute reasoning performance to individual examples, sequences, and tokens. The aim is to replace purely heuristic data selection with a more detailed account of which properties contribute to useful learning.

The analysis finds different patterns across domains. Difficult mathematics examples help both mathematics and code reasoning, while easier code tasks provide the strongest benefit for code reasoning. Guided by these findings, the authors reweight data by flipping task difficulty. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, this doubles AIME24 accuracy from 10% to 20% and raises LiveCodeBench accuracy from 33.8% to 35.3%.

Finer-grained attribution finds that exploratory behavior within reasoning sequences helps both domains. At the token level, mathematics places greater emphasis on natural-language logical connectors, while coding emphasizes structural syntax. These results show why a single rule about difficulty or token content may overlook useful distinctions. The paper connects attribution analysis to a concrete reweighting strategy with measured improvements for the evaluated model.
neurips-2025-which-data-attributes-stimu.tldr: Infra links reasoning gains to specific training-data attributes and uses domain-dependent difficulty reweighting to improve math and coding accuracy.
